title: Μῶλυ καὶ ὅρκος
titleEn: The Moly and the Oath — Odyssey 10.274–374
about: Odysseus, still telling his tale to the Phaeacians, goes up alone toward Circe’s house, and on the way a young man takes him by the hand: it is Hermes. He tells Odysseus that the crew are penned like pigs, gives him a plant called moly to protect him from Circe’s drink, and tells him what to do: draw his sword when she strikes him with her wand, accept her bed, but first make her swear a great oath not to harm him. Odysseus goes in, drinks the mixture and is not enchanted, and rushes at her with the sword. Circe recognises him from Hermes’s old prophecy and offers her bed as a pledge of trust. Odysseus repeats Hermes’s warning and demands the oath; she swears it, and he goes to bed with her. Four attendants then prepare a bath and a table, but Odysseus will not eat, his mind elsewhere and his heart foreboding evil.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν παρὰ νηὸς ἀνήιον ἠδὲ θαλάσσης.
sentences.l: So having spoken, from the ship I went up, and from the sea.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and went up from the ship and the sea.
sentences.n: ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes Odysseus’s answer to Eurylochus at 271–273; ὥς with the circumflex is the adverb ‘thus’. ἀνήιον is the imperfect of ἄνειμι ‘go up’ (from εἶμι ‘go’), ‘I went up’ inland from the shore; παρὰ νηός is ‘from beside the ship’, and ἠδέ is ‘and’ (= καί). Odysseus is still telling his tale to Alcinous, so no quotation mark opens here.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ὅτε δὴ ἄρ’ ἔμελλον ἰὼν ἱερὰς ἀνὰ βήσσας
Κίρκης ἵξεσθαι πολυφαρμάκου ἐς μέγα δῶμα,
sentences.l:
But when then I was about, going up through the sacred glens,
to reach the great house of Circe of many drugs,
sentences.i: But just as I was about to reach the great house of Circe, skilled in many drugs, as I went up through the sacred glens,
sentences.n: ἔμελλον with a future infinitive (ἵξεσθαι, from ἱκνέομαι ‘arrive at’) means ‘I was about to’, and ἰών is the participle of εἶμι. βήσσας is the accusative plural of βῆσσα ‘glen, wooded valley’; ἀνά with the accusative is ‘up through’. πολυφαρμάκου is ‘of many drugs’ (πολύς + φάρμακον): φάρμακον covers drug, charm and poison alike, and the compound marks Circe as one who knows many of them. The sentence is left hanging at the comma and finishes in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα μοι Ἑρμείας χρυσόρραπις ἀντεβόλησεν
ἐρχομένῳ πρὸς δῶμα, νεηνίῃ ἀνδρὶ ἐοικώς,
πρῶτον ὑπηνήτῃ, τοῦ περ χαριεστάτη ἥβη·
sentences.i: There Hermes of the golden wand met me as I was going toward the house, in the likeness of a young man with his first beard, at the age when youth is most graceful;
sentences.n: Ἑρμείας is the epic form of Ἑρμῆς, and χρυσόρραπις ‘of the golden wand’ is his standing epithet. ἀντεβόλησεν ‘met’ takes the dative μοι, and ἐρχομένῳ ‘as I went’ agrees with μοι. ἐοικώς, perfect participle of ἔοικα, is ‘like, resembling’ and takes the dative νεηνίῃ ἀνδρί. ὑπηνήτῃ is ‘bearded’ (ὑπήνη ‘beard’), with πρῶτον ‘for the first time’ before it; τοῦ is relative, ‘whose’, and περ sharpens it to ‘just that age’. Odysseus, as narrator, names the young man at once.

sentences.t: ἔν τ’ ἄρα μοι φῦ χειρί, ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζε·
sentences.l: and clasped me by the hand, and spoke a word, and called me by name:
sentences.i: took my hand, and spoke, calling me by name:
sentences.n: A fixed formula of gesture and address, with οἱ ‘to him’ replaced by μοι ‘to me’. ἔν … φῦ is tmesis, a preverb standing apart from its verb: ἐνέφυ ‘grew into’, so ‘clung to my hand’, took it firmly. ἔφατ’ is ἔφατο ‘he spoke’, a middle form with active sense, and ἔκ … ὀνόμαζε is a second tmesis (ἐξονομάζω ‘call by name’); ὀνόμαζε has dropped its augment, as Homer’s past tenses often do. The unit stops at the ano teleia and the speech itself begins in the next.

sentences.t:
πῇ δὴ αὖτ’, ὦ δύστηνε, δι’ ἄκριας ἔρχεαι οἶος,
χώρου ἄιδρις ἐών;
sentences.l:
‘Where now again, O wretched one, through the hilltops do you go alone,
of the place ignorant being?
sentences.i: ‘Where are you off to this time, wretched man, alone over the hilltops, with no knowledge of the place?
sentences.n: Hermes speaks; the Greek prints no quotation marks. ἔρχεαι is the uncontracted second person (= ἔρχῃ), and ἐών is the epic participle (= ὤν). αὖτε ‘again, this time’ gives the question the sense of a repeated folly. ὦ δύστηνε is the vocative of δύστηνος ‘wretched’. ἄκριας is the accusative plural of ἄκρις ‘hilltop’, and δι’ ‘through’ governs it. ἄιδρις is ‘ignorant’ (ἀ- + ἴδρις ‘knowing’) and takes the genitive χώρου ‘of the place’. The question ends mid-line, at the semicolon, and the next unit starts in the same line.

sentences.t:
ἕταροι δέ τοι οἵδ’ ἐνὶ Κίρκης
ἔρχαται ὥς τε σύες πυκινοὺς κευθμῶνας ἔχοντες.
sentences.l:
but these companions of yours, in Circe’s,
are penned, like swine, keeping solid hiding-places.
sentences.i: but these companions of yours are shut up in Circe’s house like pigs, in their solid sties.
sentences.n: τοι is σοι ‘your’, and οἵδ’ is ‘these here’. ἐνὶ Κίρκης has no noun: ‘in Circe’s (house)’, the genitive of the owner standing for the dwelling. ἕταροι is the same word as ἑταῖροι ‘companions’. ἔρχαται is the perfect passive of εἴργω ‘shut in’, in its Ionic third-plural form (= εἰργμένοι εἰσί). ὥς τε is ‘just like’ (epic τε), and σύες is the nominative plural of σῦς ‘pig’. κευθμῶνας comes from κεύθω ‘hide’: a hiding-place, here a sty. Hermes says outright what has been done to the crew.

sentences.t: ἦ τοὺς λυσόμενος δεῦρ’ ἔρχεαι;
sentences.l: Is it, them to release, that here you come?
sentences.i: Is it to free them that you have come here?
sentences.n: ἦ opens a yes-or-no question; τοὺς is the old pronoun ‘them’, not the article. λυσόμενος is the future middle participle of λύω, expressing purpose: ‘to release them’ (the middle suggests getting them free for oneself, as with a ransom). δεῦρ’ is δεῦρο ‘here, hither’, and ἔρχεαι is again the uncontracted ἔρχῃ.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σέ φημι
αὐτὸν νοστήσειν, μενέεις δὲ σύ γ’, ἔνθα περ ἄλλοι.
sentences.l:
and not you, I say,
yourself, will return home, but you will stay, you, just where the others are.
sentences.i: I tell you, you will not get home yourself; you will stay just where the others are.
sentences.n: φημι takes an accusative and infinitive: σέ … νοστήσειν ‘that you will return’, with αὐτόν ‘yourself’ placed after. μενέεις is the uncontracted future (= μενεῖς). The pronoun σύ is added for contrast, and γε sharpens it; ἔνθα περ ἄλλοι ‘just where the others (are)’ leaves out the verb.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή σε κακῶν ἐκλύσομαι ἠδὲ σαώσω.
sentences.l: But come now, from evils I will release you and I will save you.
sentences.i: But come now, I will free you from your troubles and save you.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή ‘but come now’ introduces a proposal; ἄγε is an imperative used as an interjection. ἐκλύσομαι is the future middle of ἐκλύω, here with the genitive κακῶν ‘from evils’; σαώσω is the future of σαόω ‘save, keep safe’. ἠδέ is ‘and’.

sentences.t:
τῆ, τόδε φάρμακον ἐσθλὸν ἔχων ἐς δώματα Κίρκης
ἔρχευ, ὅ κέν τοι κρατὸς ἀλάλκῃσιν κακὸν ἦμαρ.
sentences.l:
Here, this good drug having, to the halls of Circe
go, which will ward off from your head the evil day.
sentences.i: Here, take this good drug and go with it to the halls of Circe; it will keep the evil day from your head.
sentences.n: τῆ is ‘here, take this’, with the giving gesture. ἔχων ‘having’ goes with the imperative ἔρχευ (the Ionic contraction of ἔρχεο, = Attic ἔρχου). The relative ὅ is the drug, and κέν is the particle κε(ν) = ἄν. ἀλάλκῃσιν is a subjunctive of ἀλαλκεῖν ‘ward off’, in a form with the added ending -σιν. κρατός is the genitive of κάρη ‘head’ (stem κρατ-), and κακὸν ἦμαρ is ‘the evil day’, the day of ruin.

sentences.t: πάντα δέ τοι ἐρέω ὀλοφώια δήνεα Κίρκης.
sentences.l: And everything to you I will tell, the baneful designs of Circe.
sentences.i: I will tell you all of Circe’s baneful designs.
sentences.n: ἐρέω is the future ‘I will tell’, uncontracted (= ἐρῶ). δήνεα are ‘designs, counsels’. ὀλοφώια is ‘baneful’; its formation is uncertain (perhaps from ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’), so the sense is taken from context. Πάντα is separated from its noun and stands first for emphasis.

sentences.t: τεύξει τοι κυκεῶ, βαλέει δ’ ἐν φάρμακα σίτῳ.
sentences.l: She will make for you a stirred drink, and will cast drugs into the food.
sentences.i: She will make you a mixed drink and put drugs into the food.
sentences.n: τεύξει is the future of τεύχω ‘make’. κυκεών (accusative κυκεῶ) is a mixture stirred up, from κυκάω ‘stir’; it is a drink, and here nothing is said of its ingredients. βαλέει is the uncontracted future of βάλλω (= βαλεῖ); ἐν … σίτῳ ‘into the food’ is split by δ’ and the object φάρμακα. φάρμακα is the plural of φάρμακον ‘drug’. Hermes says the drugs go into the food; at 317 Circe puts the drug into the cup.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ οὐδ’ ὣς θέλξαι σε δυνήσεται·
sentences.l: But not even so will she be able to enchant you;
sentences.i: But even so she will not be able to enchant you;
sentences.n: οὐδ’ ὥς is ‘not even so’: ὥς with the accent is the adverb ‘thus’. θέλξαι is the aorist infinitive of θέλγω ‘charm, enchant’, the verb of Circe’s power. δυνήσεται is the future of δύναμαι.

sentences.t:
οὐ γὰρ ἐάσει
φάρμακον ἐσθλόν, ὅ τοι δώσω, ἐρέω δὲ ἕκαστα.
sentences.l:
for will not allow it
the good drug, which I will give you, and I will tell you each thing.
sentences.i: for the good drug I will give you will not let it happen, and I will tell you every detail.
sentences.n: ἐάσει is the future of ἐάω ‘allow, permit’; its subject is φάρμακον ἐσθλόν, and the thing allowed (the enchantment) is left unsaid. ὅ τοι δώσω: τοι is σοι, and ὅ is the neuter relative ‘which’. ἕκαστα is ‘each thing’, every particular.

sentences.t:
ὁππότε κεν Κίρκη σ’ ἐλάσῃ περιμήκεϊ ῥάβδῳ,
δὴ τότε σὺ ξίφος ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
Κίρκῃ ἐπαῖξαι, ὥς τε κτάμεναι μενεαίνων.
sentences.l:
Whenever Circe strikes you with her very long wand,
then you, the sharp sword drawing from beside your thigh,
at Circe rush, like one eager to kill.
sentences.i: When Circe strikes you with her very long wand, then draw your sharp sword from beside your thigh and rush at her as if you meant to kill her.
sentences.n: ὁππότε κεν with the subjunctive ἐλάσῃ is ‘whenever (she) strikes’ (κε(ν) = ἄν); περιμήκεϊ is ‘very long’ (περί intensive + μῆκος). ἐρυσσάμενος is the aorist middle participle of ἐρύω ‘draw’, with doubled σσ; παρὰ μηροῦ is ‘from beside the thigh’. ἐπαῖξαι is an infinitive standing in for an imperative (‘you are to rush’), as the infinitives of the following lines also do. κτάμεναι is ‘to kill’ (= κτεῖναι), and ὥς τε … μενεαίνων is ‘as if bent on’ it. Line 295 is metrically irregular as transmitted: the short first syllable of ἐπαῖξαι must be read long to open the second foot, and the -ῃ of Κίρκῃ and the -αι of ἐπαῖξαι stay long in hiatus.

sentences.t: ἡ δέ σ’ ὑποδείσασα κελήσεται εὐνηθῆναι·
sentences.l: and she, taking fright, will bid you to lie with her;
sentences.i: In fear she will bid you lie with her;
sentences.n: ἡ is the old pronoun ‘she’. ὑποδείσασα is the aorist participle of ὑποδείδω ‘shrink in fear’, ‘having taken fright’. κελήσεται is the future middle of κέλομαι ‘bid, call upon’, and εὐνηθῆναι the aorist passive infinitive of εὐνάω ‘put to bed, lay down’: here ‘to lie with her’.

sentences.t:
ἔνθα σὺ μηκέτ’ ἔπειτ’ ἀπανήνασθαι θεοῦ εὐνήν,
ὄφρα κέ τοι λύσῃ θ’ ἑτάρους αὐτόν τε κομίσσῃ·
sentences.l:
Then you no longer, thereafter, refuse the goddess’s bed,
so that she may release your companions and care for you yourself;
sentences.i: Then you must no longer refuse the goddess’s bed, so that she may free your companions and care for you yourself;
sentences.n: ἔνθα here is ‘then, at that point’. ἀπανήνασθαι, the aorist infinitive of ἀπαναίνομαι ‘refuse’, again stands for an imperative, now with μηκέτ’ ‘no longer’. θεοῦ is the masculine form used of a goddess: θεός can be either. ὄφρα κε with the subjunctives λύσῃ and κομίσσῃ is ‘so that she may’; κομίζω is ‘care for, tend’, the word for looking after a guest or a ward, and αὐτόν τε is ‘and you yourself’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλὰ κέλεσθαί μιν μακάρων μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμόσσαι,
μή τί τοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο,
μή σ’ ἀπογυμνωθέντα κακὸν καὶ ἀνήνορα θήῃ.
sentences.l:
But bid her swear the great oath of the blessed ones,
that she will not plan some other evil woe against you yourself,
lest, stripped, base and unmanned she make you.’
sentences.i: But have her swear the great oath of the blessed gods, that she will not plan some other evil woe against you, lest, when you are stripped, she make you base and unmanned.’
sentences.n: κέλεσθαι is another infinitive for an imperative; μιν is the accusative ‘her’. μακάρων ‘of the blessed ones’ means the gods, so the oath is the one the gods themselves swear. In μή τί τοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο, τοι is σοι, μή with a future infinitive gives the content of the oath ‘that she will not’, and ἄλλο ‘some other (woe)’. μή σε … θήῃ is ‘lest she make you’ (θήῃ is a subjunctive of τίθημι). ἀπογυμνωθέντα is the aorist passive participle ‘having been stripped’; κακόν here means ‘base, worthless’, and ἀνήνορα ‘unmanned’ (ἀ- + ἀνήρ). Hermes’s speech ends here.

sentences.t:
ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας πόρε φάρμακον ἀργεϊφόντης
ἐκ γαίης ἐρύσας, καί μοι φύσιν αὐτοῦ ἔδειξε.
sentences.l:
So then having spoken, gave the drug Argeïphontes,
having drawn it from the earth, and its nature showed to me.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and the slayer of Argus pulled the drug from the earth, gave it to me, and showed me its nature.
sentences.n: ὣς ἄρα φωνήσας is the formula ‘so then having spoken’. πόρε is an unaugmented aorist of πορεῖν ‘give’. Argeïphontes is Hermes under his epithet; its meaning is disputed, and ‘slayer of Argus’ is only the traditional rendering. ἐρύσας is ‘having pulled up’. φύσιν is ‘nature, growth’ (from φύω ‘grow’): what the plant is like, which the next lines give. ἔδειξε is ‘showed’.

sentences.t: ῥίζῃ μὲν μέλαν ἔσκε, γάλακτι δὲ εἴκελον ἄνθος·
sentences.l: In root black it was, and like milk the flower;
sentences.i: Its root was black, and its flower like milk;
sentences.n: ῥίζῃ and γάλακτι are datives: ῥίζῃ is ‘in respect of the root’, and εἴκελον ‘like’ takes γάλακτι ‘to milk’. ἔσκε is an epic past of εἰμί, used here simply as ‘was’ (= ἦν). μέλαν ‘black’ and ἄνθος ‘flower’ are all that is said of how the plant looks.

sentences.t: μῶλυ δέ μιν καλέουσι θεοί·
sentences.l: moly the gods call it;
sentences.i: the gods call it moly;
sentences.n: μῶλυ is a name, and its meaning is not known: the plant is not identified, and nothing in the text explains the word. καλέουσι is the uncontracted καλοῦσι ‘they call’, and μιν is ‘it’. The name is given as the gods’ word for it.

sentences.t:
χαλεπὸν δέ τ’ ὀρύσσειν
ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι, θεοὶ δέ τε πάντα δύνανται.
sentences.l:
and hard it is to dig up
for mortal men at least, but the gods can do all things.
sentences.i: It is hard for mortal men to dig up, but the gods can do anything.
sentences.n: χαλεπόν is ‘hard’ of a task. ὀρύσσειν is the infinitive of ὀρύσσω ‘dig’. τε in δέ τ’ and δέ τε is the epic τε that marks a general truth; the second clause is just such a saying. ἀνδράσι γε θνητοῖσι is ‘for mortal men, at any rate’, with γε contrasting them with the gods; θνητοῖσι has the Homeric dative ending -οισι. δύνανται is ‘are able’.

sentences.t:
Ἑρμείας μὲν ἔπειτ’ ἀπέβη πρὸς μακρὸν Ὄλυμπον
νῆσον ἀν’ ὑλήεσσαν, ἐγὼ δ’ ἐς δώματα Κίρκης
ἤια, πολλὰ δέ μοι κραδίη πόρφυρε κιόντι.
sentences.l:
Hermes then went away to long Olympus,
up through the wooded island, and I to the halls of Circe
went, and much did my heart darkly-brood as I went.
sentences.i: Then Hermes went off toward tall Olympus, up through the wooded island, and I went to the halls of Circe, my heart darkly troubled the whole way.
sentences.n: μέν … δέ sets Hermes against ἐγώ ‘I’. ἀπέβη is ‘went away’, and μακρόν is ‘long, tall’. ἀνά with the accusative is ‘up over, through’, and ὑλήεσσαν is ‘wooded’ (ὑλήεις, feminine accusative). ἤια is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘I went’. πόρφυρε is the verb used of a sea that heaves darkly, here of the heart. κιόντι is the dative participle of κίω ‘go’, agreeing with μοι: ‘to me as I went’.

sentences.t: ἔστην δ’ εἰνὶ θύρῃσι θεᾶς καλλιπλοκάμοιο·
sentences.l: And I stood at the doors of the goddess fair-plaited;
sentences.i: I stood at the doors of the fair-plaited goddess;
sentences.n: ἔστην is the aorist ‘I stood’. εἰνί is ἐνί ‘at’, and θύρῃσι is the dative plural in -ῃσι. θεᾶς is the genitive ‘of the goddess’. καλλιπλοκάμοιο is ‘fair-plaited’ (καλλι- ‘fair’ + πλόκαμος ‘plait, lock of hair’), her standing epithet; its genitive ends in -οιο (= -ου).

sentences.t: ἔνθα στὰς ἐβόησα, θεὰ δέ μευ ἔκλυεν αὐδῆς.
sentences.l: There, standing, I called out, and the goddess heard my voice.
sentences.i: Standing there, I called out, and the goddess heard my voice.
sentences.n: στάς is the aorist participle of ἵστημι ‘having taken my stand’; ἐβόησα is ‘I shouted’. μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ (= μου), and κλύω ‘hear’ takes the genitive αὐδῆς ‘the voice’ of what is heard. αὐδή is a human voice or speech.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ αἶψ’ ἐξελθοῦσα θύρας ὤιξε φαεινὰς
καὶ κάλει·
sentences.l:
And she at once, coming out, opened the shining doors
and called;
sentences.i: She came out at once, opened the shining doors, and called to them;
sentences.n: ἡ is the old pronoun ‘she’. ἐξελθοῦσα is ‘having come out’, and ὤιξε is the aorist of ἀνοίγνυμι ‘open’. φαεινάς is ‘shining’. κάλει is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘she was calling’, and has no object in the Greek: here it is Odysseus she calls. The English is the one already shipped for this identical Greek unit, where she called the crew, which is why it says ‘to them’; read it here as calling Odysseus in.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ἐγὼν ἑπόμην ἀκαχήμενος ἦτορ.
sentences.l: but I followed, grieved in heart.
sentences.i: but I followed, grieved at heart.
sentences.n: ἐγὼν is ἐγώ with a movable -ν. ἑπόμην is ‘I followed’, imperfect of ἕπομαι. ἀκαχήμενος is a perfect middle participle of ἀχέω (also ἀκαχίζω) ‘grieve’, and ἦτορ ‘heart’ stands in the accusative of respect: ‘grieved as to my heart’.

sentences.t:
εἷσε δέ μ’ εἰσαγαγοῦσα ἐπὶ θρόνου ἀργυροήλου
καλοῦ δαιδαλέου·
sentences.l:
And she seated me, leading me in, on a chair silver-studded,
fine, cunningly-worked;
sentences.i: She led me in and seated me on a silver-studded chair, a fine one, of cunning work;
sentences.n: εἷσε is the aorist of the causative ‘seat’, and εἰσαγαγοῦσα is ‘having led in’. θρόνος is an ordinary seat of honour, ‘chair’. ἀργυροήλου is ‘silver-studded’ (ἀργυρο- + ἧλος ‘nail, stud’), a genitive after ἐπί ‘on’. δαιδαλέου is ‘cunningly wrought’, the adjective from the craftsman’s art (compare Daedalus). The sentence stops at the ano teleia, and the footstool clause follows in the next unit.

sentences.t: ὑπὸ δὲ θρῆνυς ποσὶν ἦεν·
sentences.l: and beneath, for her feet, was a footstool.
sentences.i: and beneath it there was a footstool for her feet.
sentences.n: ὑπό is an adverb ‘beneath’, not a preposition, and θρῆνυς ‘footstool’ is the subject. ποσίν is the dative plural of πούς ‘foot’, ‘for the feet’. ἦεν is the longer epic form of ἦν ‘was’. The English is the shipped wording of this identical Greek unit (odyssey-002), where the seat was a woman’s; ‘her feet’ is wrong here, since the footstool is Odysseus’s (the longer unit at 366–367 says ‘my feet’). It is kept character for character only because a repeated unit must match the published one.

sentences.t:
τεῦχε δέ μοι κυκεῶ χρυσέῳ δέπαι, ὄφρα πίοιμι,
ἐν δέ τε φάρμακον ἧκε, κακὰ φρονέουσ’ ἐνὶ θυμῷ.
sentences.l:
And she made for me the stirred drink in a golden cup, that I might drink,
and in it put the drug, evil thinking in her heart.
sentences.i: She made the mixed drink for me in a golden cup, for me to drink, and put the drug into it, meaning evil in her heart.
sentences.n: τεῦχε is an unaugmented imperfect, ‘she was making’. κυκεῶ is the accusative of κυκεών; δέπαι is the dative of δέπας ‘cup’. ὄφρα πίοιμι is ‘so that I might drink’, a purpose clause with the optative. ἧκε is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send, put’, and ἐν … ἧκε is split by δέ τε (epic τε). φρονέουσ’ is the uncontracted participle of φρονέω ‘think, intend’, so κακὰ φρονέουσα is ‘meaning evil’; ἐνὶ θυμῷ is ‘in her heart’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δῶκέν τε καὶ ἔκπιον, οὐδέ μ’ ἔθελξε,
ῥάβδῳ πεπληγυῖα ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν·
sentences.l:
But when she gave it, and I drank it up, and it did not enchant me,
striking me with her wand, she spoke a word and called me by name:
sentences.i: But when she had given it and I had drunk it up, and it did not enchant me, she struck me with her wand and spoke, calling me by name:
sentences.n: δῶκεν is ‘she gave’, and ἔκπιον ‘I drank up’ is an aorist of ἐκπίνω without its augment. οὐδέ μ’ ἔθελξε has no stated subject: the drink, which is the drug at work. πεπληγυῖα is a perfect participle of πλήσσω ‘strike’, used for a single completed blow (‘having struck’), the stroke Hermes foretold at 293. ῥάβδῳ is the dative of instrument. ἔπος τ’ ἔφατ’ ἔκ τ’ ὀνόμαζεν is the same formula as at 280, now with a woman as subject.

sentences.t: ἔρχεο νῦν συφεόνδε, μετ’ ἄλλων λέξο ἑταίρων.
sentences.l: ‘Go now to the pigsty, among your other companions lie down.’
sentences.i: ‘Go now to the pigsty and lie down with your other companions.’
sentences.n: Circe speaks, and the words are the ones she would use if the wand had worked. ἔρχεο is the uncontracted imperative of ἔρχομαι (= ἔρχου); συφεόνδε is ‘to the sty’ with the suffix -δε of direction. λέξο is an aorist middle imperative of λέγομαι ‘lay oneself down’. μετ’ ἄλλων … ἑταίρων is ‘among other companions’, meaning the men already penned there.

sentences.t:
ὣς φάτ’, ἐγὼ δ’ ἄορ ὀξὺ ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ
Κίρκῃ ἐπήιξα ὥς τε κτάμεναι μενεαίνων.
sentences.l:
So she spoke, and I, the sharp sword drawing from beside my thigh,
at Circe rushed, like one eager to kill.
sentences.i: So she spoke, but I drew my sharp sword from beside my thigh and rushed at Circe as though I meant to kill her.
sentences.n: ὣς φάτο, here elided, is ‘so she spoke’. ἄορ is ‘sword’, another word for ξίφος. Odysseus does exactly as Hermes said: the participle and prepositional phrase ἐρυσσάμενος παρὰ μηροῦ and the closing words ὥς τε κτάμεναι μενεαίνων repeat Hermes’s words at 294–295. ἐπήιξα is the aorist of ἐπαΐσσω ‘rush at’, and ἐπαῖξαι at 295 is the same verb.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ μέγα ἰάχουσα ὑπέδραμε καὶ λάβε γούνων,
καί μ’ ὀλοφυρομένη ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα·
sentences.l:
And she, with a great cry, ran in under and took hold of my knees,
and to me, lamenting, winged words she spoke:
sentences.i: She cried out loudly, ran in under my sword, took hold of my knees, and, lamenting, spoke winged words to me:
sentences.n: μέγα ἰάχουσα is ‘crying out loudly’ (ἰάχω ‘cry out’). ὑπέδραμε is ‘ran in under’, inside the reach of the blade, and λάβε is an unaugmented aorist of λαμβάνω; this verb takes the genitive γούνων for the thing grasped. To clasp the knees is the suppliant’s gesture. ὀλοφυρομένη is ‘lamenting’. ἔπεα πτερόεντα προσηύδα is the formula ‘spoke winged words’, with μ’ ‘to me’ as its object; προσηύδα is the imperfect of προσαυδάω, with its augment.

sentences.t: τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν;
sentences.l: Who among men are you, and from where?
sentences.i: Who among men are you, and where from?
sentences.n: The Greek prints no quotation marks. Circe speaks again, now as a suppliant. τίς πόθεν εἰς ἀνδρῶν is the standard question put to a stranger; εἰς is the epic second person ‘you are’ (= εἶ), and ἀνδρῶν is partitive, ‘among men’. The question covers who he is and where he comes from. No opening quotation mark stands in either English layer: the shipped English of this identical unit has none and a repeated unit must match it, so the opening ‘ is left off (the closing ’ stands at 335).

sentences.t: πόθι τοι πόλις ἠδὲ τοκῆες;
sentences.l: Where is your city and your parents?
sentences.i: Where is your city, and where are your parents?
sentences.n: πόθι is the epic ‘where’ (= ποῦ), τοι is σοι ‘your’, and τοκῆες are ‘parents’. The two questions together are the usual formula of enquiry: who are you, and what is your city and family.

sentences.t: θαῦμά μ’ ἔχει ὡς οὔ τι πιὼν τάδε φάρμακ’ ἐθέλχθης·
sentences.l: A wonder holds me that, these drugs having drunk, you were not at all enchanted;
sentences.i: I am amazed that you drank these drugs and were not enchanted at all;
sentences.n: θαῦμά μ’ ἔχει is ‘wonder holds me’, an idiom for ‘I am amazed’. ὡς here is ‘that’. οὔ τι ‘not at all’ stands before πιών ‘having drunk’ but negates ἐθέλχθης, the aorist passive of θέλγω ‘enchant’. τάδε φάρμακ’ is ‘these drugs’, the plural again.

sentences.t:
οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδέ τις ἄλλος ἀνὴρ τάδε φάρμακ’ ἀνέτλη,
ὅς κε πίῃ καὶ πρῶτον ἀμείψεται ἕρκος ὀδόντων.
sentences.l:
For not even any other man these drugs has endured,
who drinks, and first passes the fence of the teeth.
sentences.i: For no other man has ever withstood these drugs, once he has drunk them and let them first pass the fence of his teeth.
sentences.n: οὐδὲ γὰρ οὐδέ τις ἄλλος is ‘for not even any other’, the second οὐδέ strengthening the first. ἀνέτλη is the aorist of ἀνατλῆναι ‘endure, hold up under’. ὅς κε πίῃ is ‘whoever drinks’ (a general relative with κε and the subjunctive). ἀμείψεται is ‘passes, crosses’, and ἕρκος ὀδόντων ‘the fence of the teeth’ is Homer’s picture of the barrier at the mouth; the drink must cross it.

sentences.t: σοὶ δέ τις ἐν στήθεσσιν ἀκήλητος νόος ἐστίν.
sentences.l: But in you some mind within your breast is not-to-be-charmed.
sentences.i: But you have some mind in your breast that cannot be charmed.
sentences.n: σοί is the dative ‘in you, you have’; τις goes with νόος ‘some mind’. ἀκήλητος is ‘not to be charmed’ (ἀ- + κηλέω ‘charm, soothe’), from κηλέω, a different verb from the θέλγω of the lines before, though the sense is the same. στήθεσσιν is the dative plural ending in -εσσιν, ‘in the breast’.

sentences.t:
ἦ σύ γ’ Ὀδυσσεύς ἐσσι πολύτροπος, ὅν τέ μοι αἰεὶ
φάσκεν ἐλεύσεσθαι χρυσόρραπις ἀργεϊφόντης,
ἐκ Τροίης ἀνιόντα θοῇ σὺν νηὶ μελαίνῃ.
sentences.l:
Truly you are Odysseus, the many-turning, whom to me always
kept saying would come the one of the golden wand, Argeïphontes,
coming back from Troy with a swift black ship.
sentences.i: Surely you are Odysseus of many shifts, whom the slayer of Argus, of the golden wand, always told me would come back from Troy in a swift black ship.
sentences.n: ἦ σύ γ’ is ‘truly you’, with γε for emphasis. ἐσσί is the epic ‘you are’ (= εἶ). πολύτροπος is a disputed epithet: ‘much-turned’, that is much-travelled, or ‘of many turns’, that is versatile. ὅν τέ μοι αἰεί is a relative ‘whom to me always’ (epic τε; αἰεί = ἀεί). φάσκεν is the unaugmented imperfect of φάσκω ‘say, assert’ (an extended form of φημί), ‘kept saying’, with the future infinitive ἐλεύσεσθαι ‘would come’; so Hermes had told Circe long before. ἀνιόντα is ‘coming back, going up’ from ἄνειμι, and θοῇ σὺν νηὶ μελαίνῃ is ‘with a swift black ship’.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ ἄγε δὴ κολεῷ μὲν ἄορ θέο, νῶι δ’ ἔπειτα
εὐνῆς ἡμετέρης ἐπιβείομεν, ὄφρα μιγέντε
εὐνῇ καὶ φιλότητι πεποίθομεν ἀλλήλοισιν.
sentences.l:
But come now, into the sheath put your sword, and we two then
upon our bed let us set foot, so that, having mingled
in bed and in love, we may trust one another.’
sentences.i: But come, put your sword back in its sheath, and let the two of us mount our bed, so that, once we have lain together in love, we may put our trust in each other.’
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἄγε δή is ‘but come now’. κολεῷ μέν is ‘into the sheath’, and θέο is an aorist middle imperative of τίθημι ‘put’. νῶι is the dual ‘we two’, and ἐπιβείομεν is an aorist subjunctive of ἐπιβαίνω ‘step onto’, ‘let us mount’, with the genitive εὐνῆς ἡμετέρης ‘our bed’. ὄφρα with the subjunctive is ‘so that’. μιγέντε is a dual participle of μίγνυμι ‘mix’, ‘having mingled’; εὐνῇ καὶ φιλότητι is ‘in bed and in love’. πεποίθομεν is a subjunctive of πείθω in the sense ‘trust’ and takes the dative ἀλλήλοισιν ‘one another’. Circe proposes that bodily union will make trust between them.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, αὐτὰρ ἐγώ μιν ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον·
sentences.l: So she spoke, and I then, answering her, addressed her:
sentences.i: So she spoke, and I answered her and said:
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατο is ‘so she spoke’, and ἀμειβόμενος προσέειπον is the first-person reply-formula ‘answering, I addressed’. The line is identical to 10.270 and takes the same published English, which fits here, where Circe has just spoken; at 270 the same wording was kept although a man, Eurylochus, had spoken.

sentences.t: ὦ Κίρκη, πῶς γάρ με κέλεαι σοὶ ἤπιον εἶναι,
sentences.l: ‘O Circe, for how do you bid me be gentle to you,
sentences.i: ‘Circe, how can you bid me be gentle toward you,
sentences.n: Odysseus answers; the Greek prints no quotation marks. πῶς γάρ ‘for how?’ gives indignation to the question. κέλεαι is the uncontracted second person of κέλομαι ‘bid’ (= κέλῃ). ἤπιον is ‘gentle, mild’ and agrees with με, with σοί ‘to you’ the person it is directed at. The sentence runs on for five lines.

sentences.t:
ἥ μοι σῦς μὲν ἔθηκας ἐνὶ μεγάροισιν ἑταίρους,
αὐτὸν δ’ ἐνθάδ’ ἔχουσα δολοφρονέουσα κελεύεις
ἐς θάλαμόν τ’ ἰέναι καὶ σῆς ἐπιβήμεναι εὐνῆς,
ὄφρα με γυμνωθέντα κακὸν καὶ ἀνήνορα θήῃς.
sentences.l:
you who have made swine of my companions in your halls,
and me myself, keeping here, scheming with guile, you bid
to go into the chamber and to set foot upon your bed,
so that me, stripped, base and unmanned, you may make?
sentences.i: you who made pigs of my companions in your halls, and now keep me here and, scheming with guile, bid me go into your chamber and mount your bed, so that you may strip me and make me base and unmanned?
sentences.n: ἥ is the feminine relative ‘you who’, carrying on the vocative; σῦς μὲν ἔθηκας … ἑταίρους is ‘you made my companions swine’ (a double accusative). μεγάροισιν is the plural dative of μέγαρον ‘hall’. αὐτόν is ‘me myself’, and ἔχουσα is ‘keeping’. δολοφρονέουσα is ‘thinking guile’ (δόλος ‘trick’ + φρονέω). ἰέναι is ‘to go’; ἐπιβήμεναι is the -μεναι infinitive of ἐπιβαίνω with genitive σῆς … εὐνῆς, ‘to set foot on your bed’. γυμνωθέντα is ‘stripped’, and the line κακὸν καὶ ἀνήνορα θήῃς echoes Hermes’s warning at 301, which Odysseus is repeating almost word for word. It is a question, though the Greek has no question mark here.

sentences.t:
οὐδ’ ἂν ἐγώ γ’ ἐθέλοιμι τεῆς ἐπιβήμεναι εὐνῆς,
εἰ μή μοι τλαίης γε, θεά, μέγαν ὅρκον ὀμόσσαι
μή τί μοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο.
sentences.l:
Nor would I, for my part, set foot upon your bed,
unless you would bring yourself, goddess, to swear me a great oath
that you will not plan some other evil woe against me myself.’
sentences.i: Nor would I mount your bed, unless you would bring yourself, goddess, to swear me a great oath that you will not plan some other evil woe against me.’
sentences.n: τεῆς is the epic form of σῆς ‘your’. οὐδ’ ἂν … ἐθέλοιμι is a potential optative, ‘I would not be willing’; εἰ μή … τλαίης is ‘unless you were to bring yourself’ (τλάω ‘endure, dare’). ὀμόσσαι is the aorist infinitive of ὄμνυμι ‘swear’ with epic σσ, and μέγαν ὅρκον ‘great oath’ is its cognate object. The oath’s own wording, μή τί μοι αὐτῷ πῆμα κακὸν βουλευσέμεν ἄλλο, is Hermes’s at 300 with one pronoun changed (μοι for τοι). Odysseus’s speech ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἐφάμην, ἡ δ’ αὐτίκ’ ἀπώμνυεν, ὡς ἐκέλευον.
sentences.l: So I spoke, and she at once swore, as I ordered.
sentences.i: So I spoke, and she swore at once, as I had told her to.
sentences.n: ὣς ἐφάμην is ‘so I spoke’ (ἐφάμην is the imperfect of φημί). ἀπώμνυεν is ‘she swore’ (ἀπόμνυμι ‘swear solemnly’), in the imperfect. ὡς ἐκέλευον is ‘as I was ordering’, with ὡς unaccented ‘as’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεί ῥ’ ὄμοσέν τε τελεύτησέν τε τὸν ὅρκον,
καὶ τότ’ ἐγὼ Κίρκης ἐπέβην περικαλλέος εὐνῆς.
sentences.l:
But when then she had sworn and finished the oath,
then I of Circe set foot upon the very fair bed.
sentences.i: And when she had sworn and completed the oath, then I mounted Circe’s very fair bed.
sentences.n: ὄμοσεν is an unaugmented aorist of ὄμνυμι, and τελεύτησεν is ‘brought to an end’; ῥ’ is the particle ῥα ‘then’, and τὸν is the old demonstrative, here nearly the article. ἐπέβην with the genitive εὐνῆς is ‘I stepped onto the bed’, the same verb as in 340–342. περικαλλέος is ‘very fair’. Odysseus gives the whole act in one clause and moves on.

sentences.t:
ἀμφίπολοι δ’ ἄρα τέως μὲν ἐνὶ μεγάροισι πένοντο
τέσσαρες, αἵ οἱ δῶμα κάτα δρήστειραι ἔασι·
sentences.l:
And the attendants meanwhile in the halls were busy,
four, who for her throughout the house are the serving-women;
sentences.i: Meanwhile four attendants were busy in the halls, the women who do her work throughout the house;
sentences.n: ἀμφίπολοι are ‘attendants’ (ἀμφί ‘about’ + the root of πέλω ‘be busy’). τέως μέν is ‘meanwhile’. πένοντο is ‘were busy, were at work’ (πένομαι ‘labour’), and τέσσαρες ‘four’ stands in apposition. In αἵ οἱ δῶμα κάτα, οἱ is ‘for her’, and δῶμα κάτα is κατὰ δῶμα ‘throughout the house’, with the preposition after its noun. δρήστειραι are ‘women who work’ (δράω ‘do’), and ἔασι is the epic ‘they are’ (= εἰσί). The present tense sets these four apart from the story as a standing fact.

sentences.t:
γίγνονται δ’ ἄρα ταί γ’ ἔκ τε κρηνέων ἀπό τ’ ἀλσέων
ἔκ θ’ ἱερῶν ποταμῶν, οἵ τ’ εἰς ἅλαδε προρέουσι.
sentences.l:
and they are born of springs and of groves
and of sacred rivers, which flow forth to the salt-sea.
sentences.i: They are born of springs and groves, and of the sacred rivers that flow out to the sea.
sentences.n: γίγνονται ‘are born’ is present, as in the previous unit. ταί is the old demonstrative ‘they’ (= αἱ), with γε for emphasis. κρηνέων and ἀλσέων are genitive plurals in -έων (= κρηνῶν, ἀλσῶν) from κρήνη ‘spring’ and ἄλσος ‘grove’. ἱερῶν ποταμῶν is ‘sacred rivers’. The preposition ἔκ … ἀπό … ἔκ is ‘from’ three times over. ἅλαδε is εἰς ἅλα ‘to the sea’ with the suffix -δε, and προρέουσι is ‘flow forth’. The text does not call these four nymphs.

sentences.t:
τάων ἡ μὲν ἔβαλλε θρόνοις ἔνι ῥήγεα καλὰ
πορφύρεα καθύπερθ’, ὑπένερθε δὲ λῖθ’ ὑπέβαλλεν·
sentences.l:
Of them one was throwing on the chairs fine blankets,
purple ones, above, and beneath was laying a linen cloth;
sentences.i: One of them was throwing fine purple blankets over the chairs, with a linen cloth laid beneath;
sentences.n: τάων is the epic genitive plural ‘of them’, and ἡ μέν ‘the one’ begins a list of four. ἔβαλλε is the imperfect ‘was throwing’. θρόνοις ἔνι is ἐν θρόνοις, the preposition after its noun. ῥήγεα are blankets or rugs and πορφύρεα ‘purple’ (the uncontracted plural). καθύπερθ’ ‘above’ and ὑπένερθε ‘beneath’ pair off; λῖθ’ is λῖτα ‘cloth’, taken as linen, and ὑπέβαλλεν is ‘was laying under’.

sentences.t:
ἡ δ’ ἑτέρη προπάροιθε θρόνων ἐτίταινε τραπέζας
ἀργυρέας, ἐπὶ δέ σφι τίθει χρύσεια κάνεια·
sentences.l:
and the second before the chairs was stretching out tables,
silver ones, and on them was setting golden baskets;
sentences.i: The second drew out silver tables in front of the chairs and set golden baskets on them;
sentences.n: ἑτέρη is ‘the other’, used for the second of the four. προπάροιθε is ‘in front of’, with the genitive θρόνων. ἐτίταινε is ‘was stretching out’ (τιταίνω), here ‘drawing out’ the tables. ἐπὶ … σφι is ‘on them’ (σφι = σφίν, the tables), and τίθει is the imperfect of τίθημι with no augment. κάνεια are baskets, here golden ones.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ τρίτη κρητῆρι μελίφρονα οἶνον ἐκίρνα
ἡδὺν ἐν ἀργυρέῳ, νέμε δὲ χρύσεια κύπελλα·
sentences.l:
and the third in a mixing-bowl honey-hearted wine was mixing,
sweet, in a silver one, and was dealing out golden cups;
sentences.i: The third mixed heart-sweetening wine in a mixing-bowl, sweet, a silver one, and dealt out golden cups;
sentences.n: κρητῆρι is the dative ‘in a mixing-bowl’, the vessel in which wine was blended with water; ἐν ἀργυρέῳ, ‘in a silver (one)’, leaves the noun out. μελίφρονα is ‘honey-hearted’ (μέλι ‘honey’ + φρήν ‘heart’), and its sense is not certain; ‘heart-sweetening’ is the usual guess. ἐκίρνα is the imperfect of κίρνημι ‘mix’, ἡδύν ‘sweet’, νέμε ‘was dealing out’ (unaugmented), and κύπελλα are cups.

sentences.t:
ἡ δὲ τετάρτη ὕδωρ ἐφόρει καὶ πῦρ ἀνέκαιε
πολλὸν ὑπὸ τρίποδι μεγάλῳ·
sentences.l:
and the fourth was carrying water and was kindling a fire,
a big one, beneath a great tripod;
sentences.i: The fourth carried water and kindled a big fire under a great tripod;
sentences.n: ἐφόρει is ‘was carrying’ (φορέω), and ἀνέκαιε ‘kindled’ (ἀνα- + καίω). πολλόν is πολύν with the epic doubled λ, ‘a great (fire)’. ὑπό with the dative is ‘beneath’, and τρίπους is the three-footed stand and cauldron in which the water is heated.

sentences.t: ἰαίνετο δ’ ὕδωρ.
sentences.l: and the water was growing warm.
sentences.i: and the water grew warm.
sentences.n: ἰαίνετο is the middle or passive imperfect of ἰαίνω ‘warm’, here ‘was being warmed’. The verb also means ‘cheer’; here the water simply warms. δ’ is ‘and’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ δὴ ζέσσεν ὕδωρ ἐνὶ ἤνοπι χαλκῷ,
ἔς ῥ’ ἀσάμινθον ἕσασα λό’ ἐκ τρίποδος μεγάλοιο,
θυμῆρες κεράσασα, κατὰ κρατός τε καὶ ὤμων,
ὄφρα μοι ἐκ κάματον θυμοφθόρον εἵλετο γυίων.
sentences.l:
But when then the water boiled in the bright bronze,
having seated me in the bath, she washed me from the great tripod,
mixing it to the heart’s pleasing, over head and shoulders,
until from my limbs she took the heart-destroying weariness.
sentences.i: And when the water boiled in the bright bronze, she set me in the bath and washed me with water from the great tripod, mixing it to suit my heart, over my head and shoulders, until she had taken the heart-destroying weariness from my limbs.
sentences.n: ζέσσεν is the aorist of ζέω ‘boil’ with doubled σσ. ἤνοπι is ‘bright’, and ἤνοψ is an old word whose exact sense is not known, though ‘gleaming’ is the traditional guess; χαλκῷ ‘bronze’ names the cauldron. ἕσασα is the aorist participle of the causative ‘seat’ (compare εἷσε at 314): ‘having seated (me)’; ἀσάμινθον is the bath. λό’ is λόε ‘she washed’, elided. θυμῆρες is ‘heart-pleasing’, said of the mixing (κεράσασα ‘having mixed’), presumably of hot water with cold. ὄφρα here is ‘until’. θυμοφθόρον is ‘heart-destroying’ (θυμός + φθείρω), and ἐκ … εἵλετο is tmesis for ‘took out of’, with the genitive γυίων ‘limbs’.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ἐπεὶ λοῦσέν τε καὶ ἔχρισεν λίπ’ ἐλαίῳ,
ἀμφὶ δέ με χλαῖναν καλὴν βάλεν ἠδὲ χιτῶνα,
εἷσε δέ μ’ εἰσαγαγοῦσα ἐπὶ θρόνου ἀργυροήλου
καλοῦ δαιδαλέου, ὑπὸ δὲ θρῆνυς ποσὶν ἦεν·
sentences.l:
But when she had bathed me and anointed me richly with oil,
and about me a fine cloak had thrown and a tunic,
she seated me, leading me in, on a chair silver-studded,
fine, cunningly-worked, and beneath, for my feet, was a footstool;
sentences.i: But when she had bathed me and anointed me richly with oil, and thrown a fine cloak and a tunic about me, she led me in and seated me on a silver-studded chair, a fine one, of cunning work, with a footstool beneath my feet;
sentences.n: λοῦσεν ‘bathed’ and ἔχρισεν ‘anointed’ are the aorists of λούω and χρίω; λίπ’ is λίπα ‘richly, glossily’, and ἐλαίῳ is ‘olive oil’. ἀμφὶ … βάλεν is tmesis (βάλεν has no augment), χλαῖνα a cloak and χιτών the tunic worn beneath it. The last two lines repeat 314–315 almost word for word, only the comma in place of the ano teleia after δαιδαλέου; the English repeats too, except that here the footstool is ‘for my feet’ (the unit at 315 keeps the shipped ‘her feet’).

sentences.t:
χέρνιβα δ’ ἀμφίπολος προχόῳ ἐπέχευε φέρουσα
καλῇ χρυσείῃ, ὑπὲρ ἀργυρέοιο λέβητος,
νίψασθαι·
sentences.i: A handmaid brought water for the hands in a fine golden pitcher and poured it over a silver basin, for them to wash;
sentences.n: χέρνιβα is water for washing the hands, and προχόῳ a pitcher for pouring. ἐπέχευε is ‘poured over’ and φέρουσα ‘bringing’. χρυσείῃ is ‘of gold’; ἀργυρέοιο is a genitive in -οιο (= -ου), and λέβητος a basin that catches the water. ἀμφίπολος is the word translated ‘attendants’ at 348; ‘handmaid’ is the shipped wording. νίψασθαι is the aorist middle infinitive of νίζω ‘wash’ (the hands), expressing purpose; it has no subject. The English is the one already shipped for this identical Greek, where several guests were served, so ‘handmaid’ and ‘for them’ are carried over, though here the guest is Odysseus alone.

sentences.t: παρὰ δὲ ξεστὴν ἐτάνυσσε τράπεζαν.
sentences.l: and beside them she drew up a polished table.
sentences.i: and she drew a polished table up beside them.
sentences.n: παρὰ … ἐτάνυσσε is tmesis: ‘stretched (a table) beside’, i.e. drew it up. ἐτάνυσσε is the aorist of τανύω with doubled σσ. ξεστήν is ‘polished’ (from ξέω ‘plane, smooth’). The English is the shipped wording for this identical line, so ‘them’ stands where the Greek names no one; here it is Odysseus’s table.

sentences.t:
σῖτον δ’ αἰδοίη ταμίη παρέθηκε φέρουσα,
εἴδατα πόλλ’ ἐπιθεῖσα, χαριζομένη παρεόντων.
sentences.l:
And bread a revered housekeeper set beside them, bringing it,
and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what was at hand;
sentences.i: A revered housekeeper brought bread and set it beside them, and laid on many dishes, giving freely of what she had by her;
sentences.n: σῖτον is ‘bread’ (grain, hence bread). αἰδοίη is ‘revered’, from αἰδώς ‘respect’; ταμίη is ‘housekeeper’. The Greek does not say whether she is one of the four attendants described at 348–359. παρέθηκε is ‘set beside’ (παρατίθημι) and φέρουσα ‘bringing’. εἴδατα are ‘dishes of food’ (the root of ἔδω ‘eat’), and ἐπιθεῖσα is ‘having laid on’. χαριζομένη is ‘giving freely, as a favour’, and παρεόντων the genitive of the participle of πάρειμι ‘be at hand’, ‘of what was there’. The English is the shipped wording of this identical line, where ‘beside them’ names several guests.

sentences.t: ἐσθέμεναι δ’ ἐκέλευεν·
sentences.l: and to eat she bade;
sentences.i: and she urged me to eat;
sentences.n: ἐσθέμεναι is an infinitive in -μεναι of ἔσθω ‘eat’. ἐκέλευεν is the imperfect ‘she was urging’ and has no stated subject: grammatically the housekeeper of the line before, though Circe is the host who would care that he eat.

sentences.t:
ἐμῷ δ’ οὐχ ἥνδανε θυμῷ,
ἀλλ’ ἥμην ἀλλοφρονέων, κακὰ δ’ ὄσσετο θυμός.
sentences.l:
but to my heart it was not pleasing,
but I sat thinking elsewhere, and evils my heart foresaw.
sentences.i: but it did not please my heart, and I sat with my thoughts elsewhere, and my heart foresaw evils.
sentences.n: ἐμῷ … θυμῷ is the dative ‘to my heart’, with ἥνδανε ‘it was pleasing’ (ἅνδανε with its augment). ἥμην is ‘I sat’, the imperfect of ἧμαι. ἀλλοφρονέων is ‘thinking other things’ (ἄλλος ‘other’ + φρονέω), his mind far from the table. ὄσσετο is ‘foresaw, forebode’ (ὄσσομαι, from the root of ὄσσε ‘eyes’), and κακά ‘evils’ is its object. θυμῷ and θυμός end the two lines, and the heart is the one that feels and foresees.
